questions.answer: C

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match, one word or complete the table).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The price of a commodity and its quantity supplied are ______ related. (b) The supply curve slopes ______.
questions.answer:
(a) positively (directly)
(b) upward from left to right

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The graphical representation of the law of supply is the ______. (b) Market supply is the ______ of individual supplies.
questions.answer:
(a) supply curve
(b) sum

questions.q: State True or False: (a) Better technology raises cost and lowers supply. (b) Factors affecting individual supply also affect market supply.
questions.answer:
(a) False — better technology lowers cost and raises supply.
(b) True.

questions.q: Give one word: (a) The definition of supply includes price, time and ______. (b) The quantity with a seller at a point of time.
questions.answer:
(a) quantity
(b) Stock

questions.q: Complete the market supply table: at ₹10, firm A supplies 150 units, firm C 200 units and market supply is 650. At ₹11, A supplies 200, C 300 and market supply is 1,000. Find firm B's supply at (a) ₹10 and (b) ₹11.
Fill in the blanks: (a) If more firms enter the market, market supply will ______. (b) A rise in wage rate will ______ supply.
questions.answer:
(a) increase
(b) decrease

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: State the law of supply.
questions.answer: Other factors remaining constant, the price of a commodity and its quantity supplied are directly related: more is supplied at a higher price and less at a lower price.

questions.q: Three firms A, B and C supply 10, 15 and 20 kg of a commodity at ₹100. Find the market supply.
questions.answer: Market supply = sum of individual supplies = 10 + 15 + 20 = 45 kg at ₹100.

questions.q: How does improved technology affect supply?
questions.answer: Better technology lowers the cost of production per unit and raises the profit margin, so firms supply more of the commodity at the same price.

questions.q: How does taxation influence supply?
questions.answer: A higher tax (VAT, excise or sales tax) raises the cost per unit, so supply falls. A cut in tax lowers cost and increases supply.

questions.q: Explain the relation between the price of a commodity and its quantity supplied.
questions.answer: They are directly related. A higher price raises the seller's revenue and profit, so more is supplied. A lower price reduces supply.

questions.q: Draw a supply curve and give the reason for its shape.
questions.answer: Plot price on the Y-axis and quantity on the X-axis using a schedule such as ₹1 – 50, ₹2 – 100, ₹3 – 150, ₹4 – 200 units. The curve slopes upward from left to right because price and quantity supplied are directly related: a higher price brings higher profit.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Distinguish between supply and stock with an example.
questions.answer:
Stock is the total quantity a seller has at a point of time. Supply is the part of the stock offered for sale at a given price over a period.
Stock is measured at a point of time; supply is a flow.
Example: a merchant holds 820 quintals of rice on 1 August (stock) and sells 300 quintals at ₹2,300 during August (supply).

questions.q: Firms A, B and C supply 40, 50 and 60 quintals of sugar at ₹3,000 a quintal. Find the market supply. What two factors, besides price, affect market supply?
questions.answer:
Market supply = 40 + 50 + 60 = 150 quintals at ₹3,000.
Other factors: (1) the number of firms — more firms means more supply; (2) the expected future price — if prices are expected to rise, firms hold back supply now.

questions.q: Explain how the price of the commodity and government policy determine the supply of a commodity.
questions.answer:
Price: a higher price means higher average and total revenue, so firms supply more; a lower price reduces supply (the law of supply).
Government policy: higher taxes such as VAT or excise raise cost per unit and reduce supply. Tax cuts and subsidies lower cost and increase supply.

questions.q: Why does the supply curve slope upward?
questions.answer:
(1) A higher price raises profit, so firms offer more.
(2) A higher price makes sellers release part of their stock.
(3) Higher profit attracts new firms into the market, adding to supply.
So more is supplied at higher prices.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain market supply with the help of a market supply schedule.
questions.answer:
Market supply is the total quantity all firms offer for sale at a given price and time — the sum of individual supplies.
Schedule (sugar, quintals a day) for firms X, Y and Z:
₹2,800: 8 + 10 + 15 = 33
₹2,900: 9 + 11 + 16 = 36
₹3,000: 10 + 12 + 17 = 39
₹3,100: 12 + 14 + 20 = 46
Market supply rises with price. It also depends on the number of firms and the expected future price.

questions.q: How is the supply of a commodity affected by (a) a fall in the price of related goods and (b) an improvement in technology?
questions.answer:
(a) Related goods: a farmer can grow wheat or rice with the same land. If the price of rice falls, rice becomes less profitable, so the farmer shifts resources to wheat. The supply of wheat rises and the supply of rice falls. A fall in the price of a related good raises the supply of the commodity.
(b) Technology: better technology reduces the cost per unit and raises the profit margin, so firms supply more at each price and supply increases. Old technology raises cost and reduces supply.

questions.q: State the law of supply with a supply schedule.
questions.answer:
Law: other things being equal, quantity supplied rises when price rises and falls when price falls — a direct relation.
Schedule (Mohan's mangoes a day): ₹20 – 100 kg; ₹30 – 200 kg; ₹40 – 300 kg; ₹50 – 400 kg; ₹60 – 500 kg.
As the price rises from ₹20 to ₹60, supply rises from 100 to 500 kg. The supply curve slopes upward because higher prices bring higher profit, sellers release stock, and new firms enter.

questions.q: Explain the factors affecting individual supply.
questions.answer:
(1) Price of the commodity — higher price, more supply.
(2) Technology — better technology lowers cost and raises supply.
(3) Price of inputs — dearer inputs raise cost and reduce supply.
(4) Prices of related goods — if rice becomes dearer, a farmer supplies more rice and less wheat.
(5) Objective of the firm — a firm that wants to maximise sales supplies more even at lower prices.
(6) Government policy — taxes reduce supply; subsidies and tax cuts increase it.
